The verification probe $\text{probe}(\MutatingToolAction, \ToolTargetState_0)$ is an authorized read operation, authored alongside the tool, that evaluates whether the intended postcondition holds relative to an initial baseline state $\ToolTargetState_0$ captured immediately before dispatch. The optional compensation routine $\text{compensate}(\MutatingToolAction)$ provides an authorized procedure for mitigating partial or unintended side effects if execution falters.[^fn-saga-compensation-tools] The probe must be implemented ahead of time as part of the tool contract, because allowing an agent model to improvise verification queries on the fly after a timeout replaces transport uncertainty with unverified heuristic guesswork. Capturing the baseline state $\ToolTargetState_0$ before dispatch provides the reference point. For example, before appending a configuration block to a remote file, the adapter records the file's initial length and cryptographic hash. After a timeout, the probe can distinguish whether the current bytes match the baseline, match the expected appended content, or match neither. These observations do not establish which actor produced the current state or whether the original attempt can still execute; those questions require an operation-specific receipt or endpoint guarantee.

[^fn-saga-compensation-tools]: **Compensating Actions**: A compensation, the saga mechanism the introduction glossed for $\AuthorityExposureLevel_2$ grants, is a new forward action that semantically neutralizes an earlier step rather than rolling it back in place. Processing a payment refund, for instance, leaves both the original charge and the subsequent credit in the account's transaction history. For this reason, tool architectures must treat compensation as a separate authorized operation requiring its own execution budget and outcome settlement, rather than pretending the initial mutation never occurred. \index{Saga!compensation}

Observing an "unchanged" probe result justifies an immediate retry only when backed by definitive structural guarantees. The runtime must either verify that the original attempt can no longer execute (for example, because the attempt has expired under a published request-expiry rule), or rely on inherently idempotent semantics where repeat execution is harmless. Without those assurances, the delayed-attempt hazard illustrated in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-delayed-attempts remains fully active. Reconciliation probes are also distributed network calls that can time out, fail, or exceed their allotted latency budgets, leaving the state unresolved.

Under these conditions, the only sound engineering decision is to classify the action as an unsettled outcome. The runtime preserves the operation identity alongside all gathered telemetry, suppresses automated retries, and escalates the ambiguity to an administrative reconciliation pipeline or human operator. A partially applied mutation frequently requires specialized remediation; many real-world actions lack mathematical inverses, and compensation remains an independent mutation with its own potential failure modes. Downstream tasks that depend strictly on the uncertain operation must block until settlement completes, whereas independent parallel subtasks can safely continue executing.

::: {#chk-07-uncertain-effects .callout-checkpoint title="Settling an uncertain effect"}

- [ ] **Delayed attempt**: A restart times out, and a later probe sees the old state. The first attempt may still commit. What additional guarantee or evidence is needed before repeating the restart?
- [ ] **Duplicate rate**: In notebook \ref{nbk-07-settlement-budget}, reply loss doubles while request loss stays fixed. Roughly how does the daily duplicate count change, and which single change removes that path instead of shrinking it?
- [ ] **Operation identity**: The agent deliberately restarts the same container a second time an hour later. Why must that request carry a new operation ID even though its arguments are identical, and what goes wrong if the runtime derives operation IDs from an argument hash?
- [ ] **Matching state**: A probe written before dispatch finds that the intended configuration block is present after a timeout. Why does a matching current state not prove that this attempt produced it, and what baseline should the probe have captured?

:::

Whether an operation ends completed, pending, or permanently ambiguous, that disposition must reach the next model call as a concise, accurate observation, so the agent plans from what is known rather than from an invented outcome. Getting any result back into the model, even the unremarkable output of a test run that did finish, raises a resource problem of its own.

## Observation Stream Truncation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming}

An automated repair agent running a test suite may encounter a process that terminates with a definitive exit code while generating a log far too vast to fit within the subsequent model request. Conversely, a remote network operation may time out with an uncertain execution state while its local connection layer still captures valuable diagnostic telemetry. Determining the concrete execution outcome of a tool invocation and deciding what subset of telemetry to stage into the prompt are distinct systems responsibilities. An agent runtime must maintain this architectural separation rather than collapsing nuanced execution states into an opaque success or failure string.

Tool execution telemetry encounters two distinct resource boundaries on its return path. **Capture**\index{Observation capture!definition} governs the physical resources (kernel memory, disk storage, CPU cycles, and wall-clock time) spent receiving output from an external process or service. Context staging governs the logical volume of tokens admitted into the model's prompt after filtering, normalization, and serialization. A brief shell command such as `grep -rn` or an unconstrained compiler build can emit hundreds of megabytes in seconds. Without rigorous capture limits, the runtime risks buffer overruns, pipe deadlocks, or host memory exhaustion long before prompt construction begins.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The context budget that bounds the observation tokens admitted to each request is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-decision.
:::

### Bounded output capture {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-bounded-capture}

Waiting for a child process to exit before reading its standard output stalls the child indefinitely as soon as its output exceeds the operating system pipe buffer (64 KB on modern Linux kernels). Buffering all output into host memory instead lets a runaway producer exhaust RAM in seconds. An execution adapter must continuously drain its communication channels while enforcing capture limits through bounded in-memory buffers and quota-managed disk storage.

The canonical failure mode in tool execution is a **pipe deadlock**\index{Pipe deadlock!definition}, which establishes a circular wait[^fn-circular-wait-deadlock] across two bounded pipes. An adapter communicating with a child process over standard input and standard output manages two unidirectional kernel pipes. Suppose the host writes a large payload to the child's input pipe and defers reading standard output until writing completes. If the child process emits verbose startup diagnostics before consuming its input, the output pipe fills, causing the child's write call to block. Concurrently, the host fills the input pipe buffer, causing its own write call to block. Both processes sleep interruptibly while waiting for the other to read, halting forward progress until an external watchdog timer terminates the task. Resolving the deadlock requires structural decoupling. The adapter must set all file descriptors to non-blocking mode and multiplex reads and writes across an asynchronous event loop, or dedicate concurrent worker threads to drain standard output and standard error independently. Draining output streams must never block on transmitting input.

[^fn-circular-wait-deadlock]: **Circular Wait**: Coffman, Elphick, and Shoshani identified four conditions that must all hold for a deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular chain of processes each waiting on the next [@coffman1971]. Two full pipes satisfy all four, since each side holds its own buffer, cannot take the other's, and waits on it. A readiness loop removes the circular wait, because the host never blocks on one channel while the other has bytes to move. \index{Deadlock!circular wait}

An operational capture policy must also define explicit behavior when limits are reached. When incoming data exceeds a retention threshold, the runtime can either drop subsequent bytes while continuing to drain the pipe to prevent process stalls, or actively terminate the executing process. The runtime must persist telemetry recording which policy was triggered and whether byte loss occurred. Because continuously reading and discarding gigabytes of runaway output still burns CPU cycles and context-switch overhead, an output-volume limit complements execution timeouts and kernel resource controls (such as POSIX process quotas or cgroup limits) rather than replacing them. Process termination is itself an asynchronous state transition with its own failure semantics, addressed alongside cancellation mechanisms in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-governance.

Within these capture boundaries, the runtime extracts the most informative evidence for model evaluation. For software engineering and compilation workloads, preserving an initial prefix and a trailing suffix captures the critical context. Build systems print environment configuration, command invocations, and compilation flags at the start, while emitting panic stack traces, assertion failures, and summary verdicts at the very end. However, intermediate warnings or early test failures can easily be lost in the omitted middle. A production capture policy must therefore disclose the exact magnitude of its omissions, while specialized diagnostic filters can selectively extract recognized error patterns from the middle stream. @Lst-vol3-head-truncation illustrates why naive head-only truncation fails in automated workflows: in this representative test log, the panic trace and assertion failure appear only after tens of thousands of passing test cases.

::: {#lst-vol3-head-truncation lst-cap="**Where head-only truncation cuts**: The invocation context sits at the top of the log and the failure sits at the bottom. A policy that keeps only the first bytes returns the banner and passing tests and discards the panic."}
```text
$ cargo test --all
   Compiling core v0.1.0 (/workspace/core)
running 48219 tests
test engine::scheduler::test_fifo ... ok
[... 48,217 further passing tests ...]
test memory::paging::test_allocator ... FAILED
---- memory::paging::test_allocator stdout ----
thread 'test_allocator' panicked at src/memory.rs:142:9:
assertion `left == right` failed
test result: FAILED. 48218 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored
```
:::

Under a head-only policy, the model receives a nonzero exit status with zero explanatory context, forcing it to guess at root causes rather than making informed repairs. A **head-and-tail policy**\index{Head-and-tail truncation!definition} resolves this by partitioning the observation byte budget $\ObservationByteBudget$ across three components:

$$\ObservationByteBudget = \HeadByteAllocation + \NoticeByteAllocation + \TailByteAllocation$$ {#eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget}

In @eq-vol3-observation-byte-budget, $\HeadByteAllocation$ reserves space for the initial execution prefix, $\NoticeByteAllocation$ allocates bytes for an explicit truncation disclaimer, and $\TailByteAllocation$ preserves the most recent output suffix. The adapter implements this with fixed memory overhead: $\HeadByteAllocation$ bytes are captured into a linear buffer until full, after which incoming bytes feed a ring buffer of size $\TailByteAllocation$. The omission counter increases only when a byte is evicted from that ring, so bytes still retained in the tail are not counted as dropped. When the child process exits, the adapter serializes the head buffer, an omission notice detailing the exact count of dropped bytes, and the ring buffer in chronological order. Capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes (@fig-vol3-stream-ingestion).

::: {#fig-vol3-stream-ingestion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Bounded capture before staging**: The adapter drains each bounded pipe from one readiness loop, so neither channel stalls the child, and enforces a byte limit and a deadline on capture. The head fills once, the tail ring overwrites its oldest bytes, and the middle is counted but not kept, so capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes. The staged observation carries status, head, a notice of the measured omission, and tail within the byte budget $\ObservationByteBudget$; a retained record, when authorized, lets later calls read omitted ranges by handle." fig-alt="Datapath diagram. A child process writes stdout and stderr into an adapter, where both bounded pipes feed one readiness loop labeled byte limit and deadline. The loop emits an output stream of any length, drawn as a bar along a time axis: a head segment, a long hatched middle that is counted but not kept, and a tail segment. Below it, a fixed-size capture memory holds a full linear head buffer, an omission count that keeps no bytes, and a tail ring buffer that overwrites its oldest slots. The buffers feed a staged observation stacked as status, head, a dashed notice of bytes omitted, tail, and handle; below the stack, the equation M obs,max equals M head plus M notice plus M tail, and an arrow leads to the next model call, measured in tokens. A dashed retained record, if authorized, serves range reads to the handle."}
![](images/svg/vol3-stream-ingestion.svg)
:::

Line counts are convenient for display, but they offer no memory safety because a single line can span gigabytes. The runtime therefore enforces byte limits across all capture and parser buffers, and the ingestion layer truncates on valid Unicode code-point boundaries so that multi-byte characters are never split before token lengths are measured. Because the model context is billed and bounded in tokens rather than bytes, an assumed bytes-per-token ratio serves only to size $\ObservationByteBudget$ in advance. Once the observation is staged, the runtime measures it with the model's own tokenizer against the observation share $\ObservationTokenCount$ of the context budget. That token count includes schema framing, invocation provenance, exit status fields, and the truncation notice itself, leaving headroom for task history, system instructions, and generation so that tool output cannot crowd out the rest of the window.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-tool-calling-observation-budget
#| echo: false
# What: Price a bounded observation retained in a specified set of later calls.
# How: Separate an illustrative byte/token estimate from serialized payload size.
from mlsysim.core.units import MB, Mtoken, USD, byte, token
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class ObservationBudget:
    # LOAD: Hypothetical corpus, serialization, selection, and billing assumptions.
    raw_bytes = 24 * MB
    bytes_per_token = 3 * byte / token
    window_tokens = 128_000 * token
    shaped_tokens = 4_000 * token
    remaining_turns = 30
    input_price = 3 * USD / Mtoken
    cached_fraction_price = 0.10

    # EXECUTE: Only the shaped payload is eligible for the priced later requests.
    raw_tokens = (raw_bytes / bytes_per_token).to(token)
    raw_windows = (raw_tokens / window_tokens).to_base_units().magnitude
    shaped_share = (shaped_tokens / window_tokens).to_base_units().magnitude
    carried_tokens = shaped_tokens * remaining_turns
    carried_cost_uncached = (carried_tokens * input_price).to(USD)
    carried_cost_cached = carried_cost_uncached * cached_fraction_price

    # GUARD: Check the illustrative magnitudes without claiming task adequacy.
    check(raw_tokens.magnitude == 8_000_000, "raw token estimate")
    check(raw_windows == 62.5, "raw log exceeds whole window")
    check(carried_tokens.to(token).magnitude == 120_000, "selected later input")
    check(abs(carried_cost_uncached.magnitude - 0.36) < 1e-12, "uncached cost")
    check(abs(carried_cost_cached.magnitude - 0.036) < 1e-12, "cached cost")

    # OUTPUT: Derived prose numbers use shared formatters.
    raw_size_str = fmt_memory(raw_bytes, unit=MB, precision=0)
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_token.to(byte / token).magnitude)
    window_tokens_str = fmt_int(window_tokens.to(token).magnitude)
    shaped_tokens_str = fmt_int(shaped_tokens.to(token).magnitude)
    remaining_turns_str = fmt_int(remaining_turns)
    input_price_str = fmt_usd((input_price * Mtoken).to(USD))
    cached_fraction_str = fmt_percent(cached_fraction_price, style="prose")
    raw_windows_mult_str = fmt_multiple(raw_windows, precision=1)
    shaped_share_str = fmt_percent(shaped_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    carried_cost_uncached_str = fmt_usd(carried_cost_uncached, precision=2)
    carried_cost_cached_str = fmt_usd(carried_cost_cached, precision=3)
    cached_discount_str = fmt_int(round(1 / cached_fraction_price))
    _mb = fmt(raw_bytes.to(MB).magnitude, precision=0, commas=False)
    _bpt = fmt_int(bytes_per_token.to(byte / token).magnitude)
    _tok = fmt_int(raw_tokens.to(token).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    raw_tokens_math = fmt_math(rf"{_mb} \times 10^{{6}} / {_bpt} = {_tok}")
    _shaped = fmt_int(shaped_tokens.to(token).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    _carried = fmt_int(carried_tokens.to(token).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    carried_math = fmt_math(rf"{_shaped} \times {remaining_turns} = {_carried}")
```

::: {#nbk-07-observation-budget .callout-notebook title="The cost of carrying one observation through a trajectory"}
**Problem**: A hypothetical test log contains `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_size_str` of text. Assume, only for this estimate, `{python} ObservationBudget.bytes_per_token_str` bytes per token. The model's context window is `{python} ObservationBudget.window_tokens_str` tokens. The adapter instead produces a `{python} ObservationBudget.shaped_tokens_str`-token serialized observation, including its metadata, and the context policy selects that same payload for `{python} ObservationBudget.remaining_turns_str` later model calls. Assume input costs `{python} ObservationBudget.input_price_str` per million uncached tokens and cached input costs `{python} ObservationBudget.cached_fraction_str` of that price. What are the size and later input-cost consequences?

**Math**: Dividing the raw bytes by the assumed bytes per token gives `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_tokens_math` tokens, or `{python} ObservationBudget.raw_windows_mult_str` the entire window. The raw log cannot be admitted to this request. Actual tokenization depends on the specific vocabulary and input encoding; a coarse byte ratio serves for capacity planning rather than admission validation.

The shaped result occupies `{python} ObservationBudget.shaped_share_str` of the whole window, before accounting for other context and output reserve. Its later input contribution is `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_math` tokens. At the assumed prices, these later reads cost `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_cost_uncached_str` if all are uncached, or `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_cost_cached_str` if all qualify for cached-input billing. These figures exclude the initial inclusion, output generation, and all other request content.

**Systems insight**: Every staged observation incurs repeated token fees across subsequent turns that retain it in context. Its carried input is $\ShapedObservationSize \cdot \RetainingCallCount$ tokens. This is the serialized size $\ShapedObservationSize$ of this one observation (one contributor to the observation share $\ObservationTokenCount$ of each request) times the number $\RetainingCallCount$ of later calls that retain it, and systems engineers control both factors. Halving the staged payload or pruning the observation once the agent acts on its diagnostic cuts token expenditure proportionally, while cached-input billing cuts the carried cost by a factor of `{python} ObservationBudget.cached_discount_str` under the assumed prices. Aggressive observation shaping directly lowers the amortized inference cost per accepted task, $\CostPerAcceptedTask$, provided the retained evidence remains sufficient for subsequent reasoning.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The cost per accepted task, $\CostPerAcceptedTask$, is established in @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic.
:::

### Truncation notices and inspection handles {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-truncation-notices}

Once a head-and-tail policy drops the middle of a log to fit $\ObservationByteBudget$, the model needs to know whether those omitted bytes still sit in storage or were discarded at the pipe boundary. Otherwise it cannot tell whether to request the missing slice or re-run the test suite with a narrower filter. A truncated observation must therefore state what was selected, what was omitted, and whether the missing data remains retrievable, distinguishing a complete capture that was staged as an excerpt from an unrecoverable drop at the pipe. Omission figures must also reflect what the adapter actually measured: if a stream dropped packets or ended early under buffer overruns, the runtime reports that uncertainty rather than fabricating an exact byte count.

When storage policy permits retention, the runtime can spool the full raw output to an external artifact store and supply the model with an **inspection handle**\index{Inspection handle!definition}\index{Raw-payload handle!inspection handle}, the raw-payload handle of @sec-vol3-context-engineering-decision as it appears at the tool boundary, subject to the same handle rule. Instead of re-executing an expensive build or test run to view omitted output, the agent can issue secondary queries such as `read_observation_slice(handle, offset_bytes, max_bytes)` to examine targeted slices. It can also invoke a server-side regular-expression search over the retained log that returns only matching lines and their byte offsets. Retaining raw logs outside the context window shifts the engineering burden to storage governance. Because retained logs consume disk space and often contain environment variables, authorization tokens, or internal paths, the artifact store must enforce capacity quotas and eviction horizons alongside the same disclosure policies that govern the primary tool call. It must return an explicit error when a handle has expired or been evicted. Content hashes can verify that a stored log has not changed, whereas read authorization and retention lifetime remain separate runtime checks.

Structured tools can avoid post-hoc log slicing altogether by partitioning query results into pages bounded in both record count and serialized byte size, so that a single oversized record cannot overflow the response. Each page reports whether more records remain, whether a scan limit or deadline cut the search short, and which cursor resumes the query. Because authorization and snapshot isolation are independent of pagination, the contract must also state whether later pages read from a frozen snapshot or see concurrent writes.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The result envelope's completion status and continuation cursor are established in @sec-vol3-persistent-result-envelope.
:::

The placement of continuation state highlights a key systems trade-off amplified by agentic workloads: stateful server-side cursors vs. stateless client tokens. A stateful cursor maintains an open database cursor, transaction snapshot, or cache entry on the server until the client finishes iterating. However, autonomous agents abandon search trajectories routinely. An informative diagnostic on the first page often redirects the agent's entire plan, causing abandoned server sessions to accumulate until garbage collection or time-to-live timeouts reclaim them. A **stateless cursor**\index{Stateless cursor!definition} avoids server-side state by encoding the continuation position directly within the token passed to the client. Because that token travels through the model's context, where generated or injected text could alter it to reach rows outside the original query, the backend authenticates it. It serializes a query descriptor, the last evaluated sort key, and an issuance timestamp into a payload $\StatelessCursorPayload$ and returns the token $\StatelessCursorPayload \parallel \text{MAC}_{\text{key}}(\StatelessCursorPayload)$ signed with a secret server key. When the client returns the token, the backend verifies the message authentication code and expiration time, ensuring resistance against client-side tampering without consuming server memory. The trade-offs for stateless cursors are relaxed consistency and increased prompt overhead. Resumption queries typically evaluate against live data rather than an isolated snapshot, and serialized cryptographic tokens consume prompt tokens on every turn that carries them.

Bounded capture and disciplined staging keep tool output within its memory and context budgets without deadlocking the child. Fitting the bytes into a budget, however, says nothing about whether they faithfully represent what the program displayed or what the process actually did. A terminal log can be garbled by its own redraws, and a clean-looking log can come from a run that checked nothing.

## Terminal Output Normalization {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-observation-parsing}

When a command-line tool executes interactively, it redraws progress indicators with carriage returns and styles diagnostics with terminal escape sequences. Captured directly at the byte level, standard output does not represent the clean visual layout a human engineer sees on a terminal screen. Wherever possible, tool adapters should invoke command-line utilities in noninteractive or batch modes (for example, `--batch` or `--no-color`), or ideally request structured machine-readable outputs such as JSON or JUnit XML. Structured reports provide discrete test identifiers, execution timings, and explicit assertions, eliminating the brittle heuristics required to parse colored progress logs. Even so, structured formatting is a transport convention; receiving a syntactically valid JSON payload does not guarantee that the tool performed all required checks or that its outputs can be trusted without schema validation and memory bounds.

When terminal output is unavoidable, the adapter must enforce a declared normalization policy backed by a stateful virtual terminal emulator or bounded screen buffer. Removing ANSI color sequences (`\x1b[31m`) is straightforward, but naively stripping control bytes like carriage returns (`\r`) or cursor positioning sequences silently corrupts output semantics.[^fn-terminal-control-functions] Because a carriage return moves the cursor to the beginning of the line without advancing to the next, a terminal progress indicator updates by repeatedly overwriting existing text. Stripping `\r` without simulating terminal geometry causes overwritten states to concatenate. For the bytes `Running... \rFailed!`, the screen shows `Failed!` written over the start of the line (`Failed!...`), whereas naive stripping yields `Running... Failed!`, a line that never appeared. Over a long run the same error accumulates megabytes of repeated progress fragments. The adapter's parser must therefore maintain cursor coordinates across chunked streaming reads while bounding its internal buffer allocations. When an adapter supports only a subset of control sequences, it must explicitly mark unsupported or incomplete escape sequences rather than discarding them silently. Because collapsing interactive updates into a final snapshot loses intermediate state transitions, the runtime should retain the raw byte stream in secondary storage as an authoritative audit log while delivering only the normalized, bounded representation to the model context. Normalization also shifts byte positions, so the adapter records a mapping from normalized offsets back to raw offsets to keep range queries through an inspection handle aligned with the original text.

[^fn-terminal-control-functions]: **Terminal Control Functions**: The escape sequences that color and reposition terminal text were standardized in ECMA-48, first published in 1976 and adopted internationally as ISO/IEC 6429 [@ecma1991control]. Its control functions act on a presentation position on a display rather than on a stream of lines, which is why recovering what an operator saw requires emulating that display rather than filtering bytes. \index{ECMA-48!terminal normalization}

Tool adapters must preserve the provenance of standard output (`stdout`) and standard error (`stderr`) while treating stream assignments as advisory conventions. In Unix environments, programs frequently emit progress updates, debugging traces, or configuration warnings across either descriptor, and capturing the two streams through separate pipes forfeits their relative temporal interleaving. When chronological event ordering is essential for root-cause diagnosis, adapters should multiplex streams using pseudo-terminal (pty) pairs or timestamped chunk logging. In extracting diagnostics, the adapter should rely on known output formats such as compiler error lines and language tracebacks, retaining source file paths and line offsets while reporting parsing failures explicitly rather than guessing a root cause from an incomplete fragment. Normalizing terminal output cleans up presentation, but the resulting text carries no intrinsic authority. Safe serialization practices, including escaping control characters and enforcing UTF-8 boundaries, protect the agent's structural messaging format from delimiter injection, while the evidence-scope rule continues to dictate what the text actually proves.

### Process status and evidential scope {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-process-status}

Even a cleanly normalized log cannot by itself prove that a check ran. A test runner pointed at an unmatched directory filter discovers zero tests and exits cleanly with status 0. A shell pipeline run without `set -o pipefail` suffers a fatal crash in its first command while still returning status 0, because its final formatting stage succeeded. The adapter must therefore read process disposition directly from operating-system primitives, such as `waitpid` status macros or container runtime lifecycle events, rather than parsing success messages from output logs. It must still treat exit status 0 as an application convention rather than proof that every required check ran. Querying the process supervisor lets the adapter report an unambiguous exit code,[^fn-exit-status-bits] an unhandled terminating signal, or a timeout without textual speculation. Equally, observing end-of-file on standard streams does not prove that a process has finished its work, because a daemon or worker process can close its inherited descriptors while continuing to run in the background. Conversely, a broken socket or interrupted channel leaves the state of any requested side effects uncertain.

[^fn-exit-status-bits]: **Eight-Bit Exit Status**: Under POSIX semantics, a parent process inspects child termination through status macros like `WIFEXITED` and `WEXITSTATUS`, which yield only the low-order eight bits (values 0–255) of the argument passed to `exit`. A program that terminates with exit code 256 wraps modulo 256 and appears to the parent as exit status 0. Standard shells also synthesize return codes above 128 when a process is killed by a signal (for example, 137 for `SIGKILL` 9 or 139 for `SIGSEGV` 11), collapsing fatal OS signals into ambiguous numerical exit statuses. An adapter that records explicit disposition variants, such as `exited(code)` vs. `signaled(sig)`, avoids truncating or conflating these conditions. \index{Exit status!POSIX}

An API client can likewise catch an internal runtime exception, print the error payload to standard output, and terminate with code 0 because the transport exchange itself finished without an unhandled crash. Under the evidence-scope rule, the adapter treats the operating-system process status as one evidentiary signal alongside structured output payloads and the task's acceptance criteria. In a connection-pool repair, for instance, confirming that a targeted reproduction test passes on workspace revision `r18` proves only that the reproducer succeeded; it does not substantiate broader system stability or justify full patch acceptance. @Lst-vol3-observation-sanitization illustrates how an adapter packages these signals together. The adapter runs a targeted test against workspace snapshot `r18`, parses its assertions, and captures the full output stream within its retention budget, while staging only a bounded summary into the prompt context.

::: {#lst-vol3-observation-sanitization lst-cap="**A bounded result with scoped evidence**: Process disposition, tested source, check outcome, and observation completeness answer different questions."}
```json
{
  "call_id": "call_test_42",
  "scope": {"repository": "repair-workspace", "revision": "r18"},
  "process": {"state": "exited", "exit_code": 0},
  "check": {
    "target": "tests/test_pool.py::test_waiter_notified_on_return",
    "outcome": "passed",
    "broader_regression_checks": "not_run"
  },
  "observation": {
    "capture": "complete",
    "staged_view": "excerpt",
    "selection": "invocation header and final test summary",
    "text": "Target: tests/test_pool.py::test_waiter_notified_on_return\n[intermediate output omitted]\nResult: passed",
    "omission_notice": "Intermediate output omitted from this view.",
    "inspection_handle": "obs_42",
    "retention": "until this task ends"
  }
}
```
:::

Each block in @lst-vol3-observation-sanitization answers a separate question so the model cannot mistake a clean exit or a short excerpt for full verification. The `call_id` field ties the result to the turn that requested it. The `scope` field pins the evidence to workspace revision `r18`, so a pass on one commit cannot be credited to a later edit. The `check` field records that the single reproducer passed while broader regression suites were not run. Because the full log was captured but only the header and summary verdict were staged into the prompt, the `observation` block marks `capture` as complete and `staged_view` as an excerpt, and it exposes `obs_42` as an inspection handle for paginated follow-up reads. Had resource limits truncated collection at the pipe, `capture` itself would be marked incomplete with the surviving byte ranges noted. Under the grant rule, the runtime mediates every read on `obs_42`, so knowing the handle string confers no ambient authority across sessions.[^fn-handle-capability-tools]

[^fn-handle-capability-tools]: **Names vs. Capabilities**: Dennis and Van Horn's foundational capability model granted authority through possession of an unforgeable ticket or reference [@dennis1966]. Agent runtime architectures intentionally stop short of treating context-visible observation handles as capabilities. Because text in a model's context window can be logged, leaked, copied by prompt injections, or replayed across user boundaries, the runtime treats an inspection handle merely as an identifier (a name). The runtime verifies caller authorization and execution scope on each access, ensuring that possessing a handle string grants no ambient authority. \index{Capability!handles versus names}

::: {#chk-07-idempotency-recovery .callout-checkpoint title="Interpreting bounded observations"}

- [ ] **Omitted evidence**: A known failed test run has a complete retained log but only a head-and-tail excerpt in context. What can the agent infer from the absent stack trace, and what bounded inspection should it request?
- [ ] **Scoped status**: The result above reports exit code zero and one targeted pass on `r18`. Which claims does that support, and which acceptance questions remain open?
- [ ] **Instruction-like output**: A normalized log contains an instruction to upload the repository elsewhere. Which presentation checks have occurred, and why do they grant no authority for that proposed upload?

:::

Synchronous tool execution assumes the adapter can resolve process status, normalize terminal streams, and package evidence within the span of a single model turn. When operations run longer than conversational deadlines allow, asynchronous dispatch extends this same return-path contract to running jobs, tracking process lifecycles and staging bounded observations without mistaking dispatch for completion.

## Asynchronous Tool Dispatch {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async}

When an automated repair agent launches an extensive regression test suite, it rarely has any useful decision to make until the results arrive. A prompt return from that tool invocation is only an acknowledgment of receipt; the actual computation has only just begun. During the intervening minutes or hours, the agent runtime must supervise background execution, enforce resource budgets, and maintain system safety without freezing its control plane or burning inference tokens on idle waiting.

### Synchronous and asynchronous interfaces {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-mismatch}

Blocking a supervisor thread on a five-minute integration build leaves the host unable to answer cancellation signals, while returning a background job handle immediately lets the agent edit `src/pool.py` midway through the test run and corrupt the workspace snapshot under test. A synchronous tool interface blocks until execution finishes and returns its final result directly to the caller. This works well for sub-second database lookups or local checks where the agent cannot proceed without the answer. Even during a synchronous wait, worker threads must monitor process heartbeats, stream partial output, and enforce timeouts without freezing the control plane. An asynchronous interface instead decouples job submission from job completion by returning a handle representing the pending task alongside methods to inspect its status, stream intermediate observations, or await termination. This separation allows the agent trajectory to suspend cleanly without burning model inference cycles, or to continue executing independent tasks concurrently, provided the runtime isolates the background job within a fixed snapshot or copy-on-write workspace so concurrent edits cannot contaminate the run.

Decoupling task execution from model inference also resolves the serving side of the tool-wait problem named in @sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle. While a background job runs, the model generates no tokens, so the serving engine can keep, move, or discard and later recompute the trajectory's KV cache state under the paused-state policies of @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping, independently of the tool's lifecycle. Keeping an open HTTP connection or a blocked synchronous socket throughout a long build provides no caching guarantee and only ties up host network resources. When the background job completes and the trajectory resumes, the runtime constructs the next prompt, and the serving engine either recomputes attention state over the prompt prefix or restores it from a prefix cache, depending on what it has evicted.

### Job handles {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-escrow}

Once job submission is decoupled from completion, the handle returned at dispatch must keep a queued job distinct from a finished one. If an asynchronous test runner returns `"status": "ok"` as soon as a job enters the work queue, the model treats a queued test suite as a passing one. If a later status poll times out and the adapter reports `"status": "failed"`, the model rolls back a patch while the test job is still running in the background. The runtime admits a proposed asynchronous call using the same validation, authorization, and resource checks required for synchronous invocation. If the executor accepts the work, the runtime records the job's identity, owner, requested operation, applicable source revision, execution limits, and observation location. A model-visible **job handle**\index{Job handle!definition} identifies that record without exposing the executor's internal process-management interface. Under the principle of least privilege, which gives each component only the authority its current task needs, status reads, output inspection, interactive input, and cancellation each require their own explicit authorization checks. A provider-neutral dispatch acknowledgment records only the pending handle:

```json
{
  "call_id": "call_tests_1",
  "status": "accepted_pending",
  "job_id": "job_tests_18",
  "source_revision": "r18",
  "result_available": false
}
```

Here `call_id` correlates the dispatch exchange, while `job_id` identifies the accepted work for later interactions. If a mutating operation also requires a logical operation ID for retry handling, that identity retains the idempotency semantics established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency; a job ID alone supplies no deduplication guarantee. Dropping the dispatch reply across an unreliable network leaves the runtime uncertain whether the executor accepted the task, mirroring the ambiguity of a timeout during a synchronous call.

This initial acknowledgment confirms only that the executor accepted the request into its work queue; it makes no claims about whether the process has started running or whether tests have passed. Subsequent status queries can report active execution, an explicit request for user input, completion with a structured result, or failure with diagnostic details. If network partitions or host restarts make the executor temporarily unreachable, returning “last observed running” alongside “current status unavailable” preserves operational context instead of triggering a mistaken rollback.

When the result becomes available, the runtime delivers the bounded observation contract, specifying the tested revision, the checks actually executed, the process exit disposition, and any output truncation. For example, a completed test job at revision `r18` can report that `test_waiter_notified_on_return` passed. Because a child process can exit cleanly while an output buffer truncates under heavy logging, process termination and output completeness remain distinct fields in the observation contract.

### Resumption mechanisms {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-resumption}

Even when a job handle reports pending state accurately, letting the model poll a five-minute background job every five seconds spends 59 full model calls reading the same 32,768-token context only to receive `"still running"`. Systems track asynchronous job state through three primary mechanisms, distinguished by whether state detection requires model inference (@tbl-vol3-resumption-mechanisms).

| Mechanism                           | Who checks or reports status?                         | When model inference is useful                                      |
|:------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Model-directed inspection           | The model proposes a bounded status or output request | A new observation may change the diagnosis or next action           |
| Runtime polling                     | The runtime checks on a bounded schedule              | A reported change requires a decision or the final result is ready  |
| Completion or progress notification | The executor signals a relevant event to the runtime  | The runtime has obtained evidence sufficient to resume deliberation |

: **Resumption choices**: Waiting and status detection can occur outside model inference; deliberate inspection remains useful when it informs a decision. {#tbl-vol3-resumption-mechanisms}

By delegating health checks to the runtime, systems avoid redundant inference calls while retaining simple polling semantics. Event-driven notifications (such as webhooks or message queues) further eliminate polling traffic between the runtime and the executor, though they introduce operational complexity. The runtime must authenticate callbacks, correlate incoming events with job identifiers, and handle dropped, delayed, or duplicated deliveries. In practice, receiving a completion notification often acts as a trigger for the runtime to execute a validated status read, rather than treating the notification payload itself as authoritative proof of completion. Both polling and notification architectures require dedicated supervisory resources to manage pending jobs across runtime host failures.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The durable return path that lets a replacement worker recover a pending job's result after the runtime host fails is developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution-effect-reconciliation.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-tool-calling-polling
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EXTRA MODEL CALLS WHILE A JOB IS PENDING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-07-token-cost-and-inference-overhead.
# │ Goal: Isolate model-driven status overhead under equal useful work.
# │ Show: Pending call count, input/output tokens, and incremental token cost.
# │ How: Count scheduled checks strictly before completion; apply hypothetical
# │      cached/uncached input and output prices. Exclude common useful calls.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *

class PollingBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario assumptions) ──────────────────────────────────
    job_duration = Q_(300, "second")  # hypothetical fixed completion time
    poll_interval = Q_(5, "second")  # checks start one interval after dispatch
    context_tokens = 32_768  # selected input per status call, including prior status
    output_tokens_per_call = 40  # complete generated status request; no extra acknowledgment
    cache_fraction = 0.95  # hypothetical aggregate input fraction billed as cached
    input_price_per_mtok = 3.00  # hypothetical dollars per million uncached input tokens
    cached_price_per_mtok = 0.30  # hypothetical dollars per million cached input tokens
    output_price_per_mtok = 15.00  # hypothetical dollars per million generated tokens

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    pending_calls = math.ceil((job_duration / poll_interval).to("").magnitude) - 1
    total_input_tokens = pending_calls * context_tokens
    total_output_tokens = pending_calls * output_tokens_per_call
    blended_input_price = (1 - cache_fraction) * input_price_per_mtok + cache_fraction * cached_price_per_mtok
    input_cost = total_input_tokens / 1e6 * blended_input_price
    output_cost = total_output_tokens / 1e6 * output_price_per_mtok
    extra_cost = input_cost + output_cost

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Prose claims) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pending_calls == 59, "Only scheduled checks strictly before completion count")
    check(total_input_tokens == 1_933_312, "Input includes exactly the pending calls")
    check(total_output_tokens == 2_360, "No separate generated acknowledgment is charged")
    check(abs(extra_cost - 0.87639072) < 1e-8, "Incremental token cost under stated prices")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    job_s_str = fmt_time(job_duration, unit="second", precision=0)
    interval_s_str = fmt_time(poll_interval, unit="second", precision=0)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(context_tokens)
    output_tokens_per_call_str = fmt_tokens(output_tokens_per_call)
    cache_pct_str = fmt_percent(cache_fraction, style="prose")
    input_price_str = fmt_usd(input_price_per_mtok, precision=0)
    cached_price_str = fmt_usd(cached_price_per_mtok, precision=2)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_price_per_mtok, precision=0)
    pending_calls_str = fmt_count(pending_calls)
    total_input_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(total_input_tokens)
    total_output_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(total_output_tokens)
    input_cost_str = fmt_usd(input_cost, precision=4)
    output_cost_str = fmt_usd(output_cost, precision=4)
    extra_cost_str = fmt_usd(extra_cost, precision=4)
```

::: {#nbk-07-token-cost-and-inference-overhead .callout-notebook title="The extra cost of asking whether a job finished"}

**Problem**: A background test job completes in `{python} PollingBudget.job_s_str`. Under a model-directed polling strategy, the agent queries status every `{python} PollingBudget.interval_s_str`, starting one interval after dispatch and ending strictly before completion. Assume each status check finishes before the next scheduled query and does not alter overall execution time. Each model invocation consumes a `{python} PollingBudget.context_tokens_str`-token prompt (including preceding status history) and generates a `{python} PollingBudget.output_tokens_per_call_str`-token query, with no additional model acknowledgment required. What incremental inference overhead does this polling loop impose compared to event-driven runtime detection?

**Math**: Both architectures make the initial dispatch call and the final completion call, so those shared calls are excluded. The polling schedule produces `{python} PollingBudget.pending_calls_str` intermediate model invocations, consuming `{python} PollingBudget.total_input_tokens_str` input tokens and `{python} PollingBudget.total_output_tokens_str` generated tokens. The selected context length remains fixed across queries rather than accumulating unbounded history.

Assume `{python} PollingBudget.cache_pct_str` of input tokens qualify for prompt caching discounts, priced at `{python} PollingBudget.cached_price_str` per million tokens vs. `{python} PollingBudget.input_price_str` per million uncached tokens, with generation billed at `{python} PollingBudget.output_price_str` per million tokens. Multiplying token counts by their respective rates yields `{python} PollingBudget.input_cost_str` in input charges and `{python} PollingBudget.output_cost_str` in output charges, producing `{python} PollingBudget.extra_cost_str` of direct inference overhead per background job.

**Systems insight**: The overhead is $\StatusPollCount = \lceil \JobDuration/\FiniteChange \TimeInstant \rceil - 1$ status calls for a job of duration $\JobDuration$ polled every $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, each reading $\SequenceLength$ input tokens and generating $\OutputLength$. It therefore costs $\StatusPollCount(\SequenceLength\,\BlendedInputTokenPrice + \OutputLength\,\OutputTokenPrice)$ at per-token input price $\BlendedInputTokenPrice$ (here the cache-blended price) and output price $\OutputTokenPrice$. It grows linearly with job duration and inversely with the poll interval. Halving the interval roughly doubles the expenditure, and the interval also sets detection delay: a completion is noticed at most $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$ after it happens. Under model-directed polling, cost and worst-case delay therefore trade directly, since halving the cost by doubling $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$ doubles the worst-case delay, whereas runtime polling decouples the two because its checks cost no inference. The `{python} PollingBudget.extra_cost_str` per pending job is more than twice the `{python} ObservationBudget.carried_cost_uncached_str` that carrying the shaped observation of notebook \ref{nbk-07-observation-budget} through `{python} ObservationBudget.remaining_turns_str` uncached calls cost. It inflates the attempt cost in the numerator of effective cost $\CostPerAcceptedTask$, paying for status information that the host runtime can monitor at near-zero cost. Systems should delegate routine state tracking to the runtime harness, waking the model only when an incoming observation can change the next decision.

:::

### Job supervision and cancellation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-governance}

Delegating status checks to the runtime also leaves the runtime responsible for supervising the background job while the model trajectory is paused. Throughout the job's lifetime, the runtime enforces its execution deadline, resource ceilings, output budgets, and permitted external side effects, returning the latest status and a timestamped, truncation-marked output slice whenever a bounded inspection request arrives. If a job's output stream goes silent, the runtime cannot assume deadlock from silence alone; an explicit status signal or diagnostic probe is needed to tell slow computation apart from blocked I/O awaiting user input or a wedged worker process.

When a tool genuinely awaits interactive input, the runtime should avoid guessing from operating-system process sleep states. Wherever possible, adapters invoke tools in non-interactive modes with complete parameters supplied up front; when interaction cannot be avoided, an explicit adapter event or structured message must declare what prompt the job expects. Before forwarding any input from the agent, the runtime re-checks the job's state, the input's meaning, and the session's grants, because answering `"yes"` to an interactive migration prompt can trigger schema mutations that exceed a read-only inspection grant.

When a job must be stopped—whether by an explicit cancellation request or an expired deadline—the runtime treats cancellation as an asynchronous control operation with its own intermediate states rather than an instantaneous rollback. After acknowledging the cancellation request, the runtime records what the executor actually reports: the job may stop cleanly, finish before the signal arrives, reject cancellation, or become unreachable with termination unconfirmed. Reclaiming every descendant process is where naive cancellation fails. When a background job runs `bash -c "make && pytest"` and times out, sending `SIGTERM` only to the top-level shell kills the shell. It leaves `make`, compiler workers, and `pytest` running as orphaned children reparented to `PID 1`, and they still hold filesystem locks and burn CPU cycles. On a POSIX host, the containment unit for local signaling is instead a **process group**\index{POSIX process group!definition}, which groups all processes reached by a single signal. The execution adapter makes each job the leader of its own process group at spawn time by calling `setpgid(0, 0)` in the child before `exec`. It then signals the entire group with `SIGTERM` first, which gives processes a bounded grace period to flush buffers and release locks, and follows with an uncatchable `SIGKILL`. @Lst-vol3-process-group-teardown implements this escalation pattern and reports one of four verified outcomes. The outcome is `exited` when the group was gone before any signal, `terminated` when it stopped during the `SIGTERM` grace period, `killed` when it stopped only after `SIGKILL`, and `unconfirmed` when members remain after both. If an untrusted process deliberately creates a new session or process group to escape group signaling, the runtime must rely on kernel-level isolation boundaries.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Tearing down processes that detach from the task's process group, as part of a sandbox's reset contract, is developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset.
:::

::: {#lst-vol3-process-group-teardown lst-cap="**Process-group teardown with escalation**: The job leads its own group, so one signal reaches every descendant still in it. Liveness is probed with signal 0 after reaping exited children, and a group that survives `SIGKILL` is reported as unconfirmed rather than assumed stopped."}
```python
import os, signal, subprocess, time

def spawn_job(argv):
    proc = subprocess.Popen(argv, process_group=0)  # setpgid(0, 0)
    return proc.pid                  # the leader's PID is the group ID

def group_alive(pgid):
    try:                             # reap exited children of ours,
        while os.waitpid(-pgid, os.WNOHANG)[0] > 0:  # or zombies
            pass                                     # still count
    except ChildProcessError:        # no children of ours remain
        pass
    try:
        os.killpg(pgid, 0)           # signal 0 probes, delivers nothing
        return True
    except ProcessLookupError:
        return False

def terminate_group(pgid, grace_s=3.0):
    for sig, wait_s in ((signal.SIGTERM, grace_s), (signal.SIGKILL, 1.0)):
        try:
            os.killpg(pgid, sig)
        except ProcessLookupError:   # group already gone
            return "exited" if sig == signal.SIGTERM else "terminated"
        deadline = time.monotonic() + wait_s
        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            if not group_alive(pgid):
                return "terminated" if sig == signal.SIGTERM else "killed"
            time.sleep(0.05)
    return "unconfirmed"             # report it; do not claim a stop
```
:::

Two subtle POSIX semantics explain why `group_alive` pairs `os.waitpid(-pgid, os.WNOHANG)` with `os.killpg(pgid, 0)`. First, an exited direct child remains in the kernel process table as a zombie until its parent reaps it, so probing the process group before reaping would report an exited child as still alive. The `while` loop drains every direct child in `pgid` that has already exited, stopping as soon as `waitpid` returns `0` (meaning direct children still exist in the group and none is currently ready to reap) or raises `ChildProcessError` (meaning no direct children remain). Second, `waitpid` can see only the runtime's direct children. If the group leader exits while its grandchildren (`make` and `pytest`) are still running, the kernel reparents those grandchildren to `init` (`PID 1`), making them invisible to `waitpid` even though they remain in process group `pgid`. Sending signal 0 via `os.killpg(pgid, 0)` delivers no signal, yet asks the kernel whether any live process still belongs to `pgid` regardless of parent. Reaping zombies first and probing `pgid` with signal 0 afterward therefore confirms whether the entire process tree has exited.

Even when process termination is confirmed, stopping an execution does not roll back side effects that occurred before the signal arrived. A canceled deployment script may already have mutated external cloud resources, and a canceled test run may leave temporary database tables behind. The final observation emitted by the runtime must record all known side effects, pending cleanup obligations, and ambiguous states. In the system's execution log, a status of "canceled" confirms that execution halted; it does not signify that the system returned to its original state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Remediating the partial effects and cleanup obligations an interrupted job leaves behind is developed in @sec-vol3-sagas-architecture.
:::

An asynchronous interface thus carries the tool contract across time. It acknowledges queued work without stalling the trajectory, keeps resource limits and supervision in force while the model waits, returns bounded observations, and never reports a requested state as a confirmed one. Every mechanism so far has treated one tool at a time and taken that tool's presence for granted. The remaining decisions concern the whole set: which tools the model sees on a given turn, and how much work each one performs.

## Designing the Active Toolkit {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-toolkit-design}

The repair agent working on the connection-pool race in `src/pool.py` requires concrete operations: inspecting source files, applying candidate patches, executing test suites, and analyzing run-time diagnostics. Toolkit design governs how an agent runtime exposes these capabilities to the foundation model. If an interface exposes too little functionality per invocation, the model must coordinate low-level state across dozens of turns. If it exposes an unconstrained catalog, the context window fills with irrelevant tool schemas that consume input capacity and bloat prefill latency on every turn, and each extra descriptor is one more candidate the model must rule out. Whether those candidates lower selection accuracy for a given model and catalog is an empirical question that catalog evaluation (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-catalog-evaluation) measures rather than assumes. The goal of toolkit design is to expose operations so that the model can choose an appropriate next step without carrying unnecessary definitions or managing avoidable intermediate state.

Two design dimensions govern this trade-off. Granularity determines how much work an individual tool performs, while catalog selection determines which subset of tool definitions the model sees on any given turn, known as the **active toolkit**\index{Active toolkit!definition}. A small catalog can contain either narrowly bounded primitives or a broadly expressive command runner, whereas an enterprise environment registering hundreds of specialized tools must stage them selectively rather than presenting the entire catalog on every turn.

### Static and on-demand staging {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-tool-staging}

Serializing all 50 registered tool descriptors into every model call burns 15,000 tokens of context capacity on every turn even when a step needs only six tools, whereas selecting a narrow subset on demand risks omitting the one tool the repair needs next. In **static staging**\index{Tool staging!static}, the runtime serializes a fixed set of tool descriptors into every request, keeping available interfaces predictable and eliminating separate discovery steps at the cost of carrying unused schemas on every turn. In **on-demand staging**\index{Tool staging!on-demand}, the runtime dynamically selects descriptors as the trajectory unfolds, shrinking the prompt footprint and prefill latency at the risk that an omitted tool forces the agent to spend extra turns locating it.

Selection mechanisms vary widely in implementation complexity. A runtime can employ deterministic task-to-tool mappings, hierarchical namespace menus, keyword matching, dense vector retrieval, or a combination of these approaches. Dense retrieval represents one possible search technique rather than a universal requirement for large catalogs. Any match returned by a retriever is merely a candidate descriptor. A robust systems design provides a bounded fallback path, such as a dedicated tool-search operation or an explicit discovery-failure signal, so that an omitted descriptor does not cause the model to conclude erroneously that the operation cannot be performed.

Staging a descriptor makes its syntactic and semantic contract visible to the model; under the grant rule, staging confers no execution privileges. The runtime must still resolve and authenticate every proposed invocation against registered tool identities and permissions before execution. If a dynamic discovery step returns a modified or re-versioned descriptor, the runtime must reconcile that version before executing it, preventing the model from dispatching against an interface different from the one it was provided.

Tool definitions consume prompt capacity alongside system instructions, source excerpts, previous observations, and generation headroom. Systems engineers must measure the final serialized request, including formatting delimiters, wrapper schemas, and selection metadata, rather than tallying independently tokenized description fragments under the false assumption that token boundaries are free. The following notebook counts the catalog-related input for a single model request.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/tool_calling_margin_catalog_budget.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars drawn to scale. The full-catalog bar is solid. The selected bar is a short descriptor segment plus a thin selection-overhead segment, with the remaining length outlined and labeled released."}

*Selection frees most of the catalog's input, on every call.*
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: calc-vol3-toolkit-catalog-budget
# What: Compare catalog-related input in one hypothetical model request.
# How: Charge full descriptors in both layouts and explicit additional
#      selection/framing tokens in the selected layout. No hardware estimate.
from mlsysim import *

class ToolkitCatalogBudget:
    # 1. LOAD — stipulated counts in final serialization, not tokenizer laws.
    registered_tools = 50
    selected_tools = 6
    tokens_per_descriptor = 300 * count
    selection_overhead = 400 * count

    # 2. EXECUTE — other request content is held fixed and excluded here.
    static_tokens = registered_tools * tokens_per_descriptor
    selected_descriptors = selected_tools * tokens_per_descriptor
    selected_total = selected_descriptors + selection_overhead
    released_capacity = static_tokens - selected_total
    unused_descriptors = (registered_tools - selected_tools) * tokens_per_descriptor
    breakeven_unused = (selection_overhead / tokens_per_descriptor).to("").magnitude

    # 3. GUARD — compare the same descriptors and include added overhead.
    check(0 < selected_tools < registered_tools, "Selected tools form a proper subset")
    check(static_tokens == 15_000 * count, "Full catalog count must balance")
    check(selected_total == 2_200 * count, "Selected count includes selection overhead")
    check(selected_total + released_capacity == static_tokens, "Capacity accounting must balance")
    check(unused_descriptors == 13_200 * count, "Unused descriptors removed by selection")
    check(1 < breakeven_unused < 2, "Selection pays once two unused descriptors are removed")

    # 4. OUTPUT — typed counts and token formatters for every visible input/result.
    registered_tools_str = fmt_count(registered_tools * count)
    selected_tools_str = fmt_count(selected_tools * count)
    tokens_per_descriptor_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_descriptor)
    selection_overhead_str = fmt_tokens(selection_overhead)
    static_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(static_tokens)
    selected_total_str = fmt_tokens(selected_total)
    unused_descriptors_str = fmt_tokens(unused_descriptors)
    breakeven_unused_str = fmt(breakeven_unused, precision=1)
    _n = lambda q: fmt_int(q.to(count).magnitude).replace(",", "{,}")
    static_math = fmt_math(rf"{registered_tools} \times {_n(tokens_per_descriptor)} = {_n(static_tokens)}")
    selected_math = fmt_math(rf"{selected_tools} \times {_n(tokens_per_descriptor)} + {_n(selection_overhead)} = {_n(selected_total)}")
    released_math = fmt_math(rf"{_n(static_tokens)} - {_n(selected_total)} = {_n(released_capacity)}")
```

::: {#nbk-07-memory-footprint-and-prefill-latency .callout-notebook title="The input budget of an active catalog"}

**Problem**: How much next-call input capacity does a selected catalog release after counting its additional framing and selection information?

**Variables**: Suppose a registered catalog has `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.registered_tools_str` tools. Each complete descriptor contributes `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.tokens_per_descriptor_str` tokens, including its share of catalog framing. The alternative stages `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selected_tools_str` of the same descriptors plus `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selection_overhead_str` additional tokens for the selection interface and metadata. These are stipulated contributions within the final serialization, with other request content unchanged. In this scenario the runtime selects the subset without another model call.

**Math**: Full staging uses `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.static_math` tokens. The selected descriptors plus selection overhead use `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selected_math` tokens. The released capacity is therefore `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.released_math` tokens.

**Systems insight**: Selection pays whenever its overhead is smaller than the unused descriptors it removes, $(\RegisteredDescriptorCount - \SelectedDescriptorCount)\,\ToolDescriptorSize > \SelectionOverheadSize$ for $\SelectedDescriptorCount$ of $\RegisteredDescriptorCount$ descriptors of $\ToolDescriptorSize$ tokens each and $\SelectionOverheadSize$ tokens of selection overhead. Here that is `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.selection_overhead_str` against `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.unused_descriptors_str` tokens. Break-even sits at about `{python} ToolkitCatalogBudget.breakeven_unused_str` unused descriptors, so the saving grows linearly with catalog size. The released capacity recurs on every call that would have carried the full catalog, so over a trajectory it multiplies by the number of turns, like the carried observation in notebook \ref{nbk-07-observation-budget}. The comparison flips when selection needs its own model call or a missed tool forces rediscovery; those calls belong in the same token count.

:::

Static and selected catalogs also interact differently with prefix caching in serving runtimes. When an inference engine uses radix-tree or hash-based KV cache reuse, maintaining an identical serialized prefix across turns allows the engine to bypass prefill computation for earlier prompt segments. Static staging preserves a stable prompt prefix across calls, maximizing cache reuse as long as earlier conversation state remains intact. Conversely, modifying descriptors or reordering them across turns moves the point of prompt divergence earlier, invalidating downstream cached KV blocks and forcing redundant prefill computation. Caching also changes what selection buys. If the full catalog sits in a cached root billed at `{python} ObservationBudget.cached_fraction_str` of the uncached price, as assumed in notebook \ref{nbk-07-observation-budget}, the dollar value of the tokens that selection releases in notebook \ref{nbk-07-memory-footprint-and-prefill-latency} shrinks by the same factor of `{python} ObservationBudget.cached_discount_str`. The released context capacity is unchanged. Once caching applies, selection pays mainly in capacity for task evidence rather than in money. A hybrid strategy applies the change-rate ordering of @sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging to the catalog: an immutable core of common descriptors sits in the stable root of the prompt, and task-specific additions are appended later. Even so, systems designers must not retain obsolete or revoked definitions merely to retain a cache hit, as doing so exposes outdated interfaces to the model. Removing an earlier temporary tool definition also alters the prompt prefix for subsequent turns, invalidating the cached state of the assistant responses and observations that followed it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Radix-tree prefix caching and KV block reuse across prompt turns are established in @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree.
:::

### Tool granularity {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-granularity}

Whereas staging decides which tools appear on a turn, granularity decides how much operational work each call encapsulates. A file-editing interface built from separate `open_file`, `seek_cursor`, `write_bytes`, and `close_file` tools forces the model to spend four turns and manage raw file descriptors, cursor offsets, and cleanup across the trajectory only to apply a one-line patch. Classic systems modularity principles apply directly here. Parnas established that effective module boundaries hide design decisions that are subject to change [@parnas1972criteria]. Ousterhout formalized this criterion through deep vs. shallow interfaces, measuring how much implementation complexity an abstraction hides relative to the surface area it exposes [@ousterhout2018philosophy]. The same principles hold in agent systems, where tool interfaces designed around an agent's editing, navigation, and testing patterns raised task success rates on software engineering benchmarks [@yang2024sweagent]. A **deep interface**\index{Deep interface!definition} encapsulates substantial functionality behind a concise contract, whereas a shallow interface exposes almost as much complexity as it implements. Decomposing a file edit into `open_file`, `seek_cursor`, `write_bytes`, and `close_file` is warranted only when intermediate inspection is an explicit requirement.

A task-level patch operation moves mechanical file manipulation behind the tool implementation, returning a unified diff, a resulting version hash, or an explicit conflict. The conditional-edit contract in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas illustrates this boundary. However, interface naming alone does not guarantee transactional safety. If an operation advertises all-or-nothing execution, the underlying implementation must enforce that atomicity across its mutation scope and failure modes. When operations span multiple files or distributed endpoints, partial side effects can occur, and the runtime must report those partial outcomes explicitly in the tool observation. Bundling multi-step work into a single tool call reallocates responsibility from model planning to runtime execution, but the underlying systems obligations remain intact. For the same edit, the shallow composition spends four model calls where the task-level operation spends one (@fig-vol3-deep-vs-shallow-interface).

::: {#fig-vol3-deep-vs-shallow-interface fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Shallow and deep interfaces for one edit**: The low-level composition (a) spends four model calls and places a handle, a cursor, and cleanup in the trajectory between them. The task-level operation (b) spends one call and moves the version check and the change behind the interface, returning either a diff with its new version or a version conflict. The deeper interface is all-or-nothing only if its implementation provides that property; either way, the obligations move rather than disappear." fig-alt="Two stacked panels, each with a trajectory row above a dashed interface line and a tool row below it. Panel a, low-level composition, labeled 4 model calls: four call boxes along the trajectory, each with a round trip down to one tool operation, open_file, seek_cursor, write_bytes, and close_file; small chips between the calls carry a handle, a cursor, and cleanup along the trajectory. Panel b, task-level operation, labeled 1 model call: one call box goes down to a single apply_patch operation that contains check version followed by apply change; check version returns a version conflict and apply change returns a diff and new version, both back above the interface line."}
![](images/svg/deep_vs_shallow_tool_interface.svg)
:::

Careful toolkit design does not require eliminating all overlapping capabilities. A system can effectively combine a structured search tool that returns abstract syntax tree (AST) matches with an authorized shell runner that supports complex log analysis beyond the search tool's schema. To prevent model confusion, their descriptors must articulate clear functional boundaries, target inputs, and operational limits. Providing duplicate tools with near-identical names and indistinguishable schemas adds selection noise without expanding capability; in contrast, providing complementary interfaces with distinct observation formats, coverage scopes, or authorization grants offers substantial utility. @Tbl-vol3-toolkit-granularity summarizes how these interface styles partition responsibility between the model and runtime.

| Interface style                   | Work assigned to the model                                   | Work assigned to the implementation                                                           |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Low-level composition             | Select intermediate operations and manage their dependencies | Validate each operation and expose handle, status, and cleanup semantics.                     |
| Task-level operation              | Specify a bounded intent, such as a patch or a test target   | Implement preconditions, mutation boundaries, and interpretable results for that task.        |
| General command or program runner | Construct a program that expresses the intended work         | Enforce execution grants and resource limits, supervise the job, and return bounded evidence. |

: **Toolkit granularity and responsibility**: Broader composition and task-specific interfaces place different obligations on the model and implementation; neither column substitutes for authorization or containment. {#tbl-vol3-toolkit-granularity tbl-colwidths="[24,33,43]"}

An argument schema constrains the syntactic format of a request, but it cannot constrain the underlying code execution. A specialized symbol-renaming tool may parse external ASTs, inspect secondary source trees, or execute defective third-party libraries. A narrow signature provides safety only when the implementation and its surrounding execution sandbox enforce that advertised boundary. Conversely, a shell runner's blast radius is defined by its working directory, operating-system privileges, credential access, and network egress rules. Because the side effects of an expressive shell command cannot be reliably determined by inspecting its arguments, the runtime must rely on containment to enforce isolation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The isolation envelope that enforces a command's reach regardless of its arguments is developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms.
:::

Tool implementations should also adopt defensive defaults that fail visibly. When an agent provides an ambiguous file path or target identifier, rejecting the call with an informative diagnostic is far safer than guessing or silently appending data, as appending is a stateful mutation that can silently duplicate configuration entries. A dry-run mode allows the model to inspect a proposed diff against the current workspace state before committing changes; the runtime must still enforce approval gates and verify preconditions at execution time. These defensive defaults make operational failures interpretable, but engineers should remember that rollback capabilities and high-fidelity simulation are properties of the underlying tool implementation, not inherent guarantees of the interface.

### Catalog evaluation {#sec-vol3-tool-calling-catalog-evaluation}

Choosing between those granularity and staging options requires measuring end-to-end trajectories rather than single-step accuracy. Comparing a 12-tool structured catalog against a single `run_shell` tool by tool-selection accuracy alone makes the shell runner look superior, because the model cannot pick the wrong tool name out of a catalog of one. That comparison hides the unconfined mutations and recovery turns the shell introduces. Evaluating toolkit designs therefore requires holding all other experimental factors constant (the benchmark task distribution, initial workspace snapshots, model checkpoints, generation parameters, token budgets, and verification suites). The trials must also exercise realistic failure modes across the connection-pool repair workload. These include locating relevant source files across deep directory hierarchies, applying patches against concurrently modified buffers, interpreting noisy test failure logs, and recovering when a needed descriptor is omitted from the initial active toolkit.
